verses.translation_literal: Why, YHWH, do you stand in distance? [Why] do you hide to times in the trouble?
verses.translation_dramatic: Why, LORD, do you stand so far away? Why do you hide your face just when the trouble comes?
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens not with praise but with an accusation shaped as a question: 'Why?' (lāmâ) is the voice of the lament genre, and it is addressed straight to God, who is expected to be near. The picture is spatial and almost physical: God 'standing' (ʿāmad) at a distance, like a bystander at the edge of a crowd who sees the assault and does not move. The KJV 'afar off' and 'hidest thou thyself' are close, but 'thyself' is added; the verb taʿlîm means 'you conceal [yourself or your eye]', and Rashi supplies 'eyes': you shut your eyes in times of trouble. Notice 'in the trouble' carries a definite article; the singular 'trouble' is the distress of this speaker, not a general idea. Ancient listeners, who knew the temple as the place where God drew near, would hear this as a charge that the divine king has left the field. Directors: play it quietly, not with rage; the anger is in the restraint.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of ʿālam, 'to hide, conceal'. Elsewhere the object is 'the eyes' (Lev 20:4), which is the sense Rashi spells out; the KJV 'hidest thou thyself' adds a reflexive the Hebrew does not have.
'at times in the distress'. The plural 'times' with the singular 'trouble' recurs in Ps 9:10; the phrase marks the moments when help is most urgent.

verses.translation_literal: In the pride of a wicked one he burns after the afflicted; they are caught in the schemes which they have planned.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the pride of the wicked the poor are hunted, burned along behind him like a fire. Let them be caught in the very schemes they have devised.
verses.directors_commentary: Two voices speak here, or one voice that turns from description to prayer. The first line states the facts: the proud rich man 'burns' (yidlaq) after the poor. The verb is literally 'to be hot, to burn', and it also means 'to pursue hotly', as when Laban 'burned after' Jacob (Gen 31:36), the parallel Rashi and Meiri both give. The KJV 'doth persecute' flattens the image of fire in pursuit; YLT 'is inflamed' keeps the burn but loses the chase. The second line is ambiguous in number and mood: 'they are caught' can be a statement or a wish. Radak, Meiri and the KJV read it as a prayer ('let them be taken'); Rashi reads it as the poor who are caught. The pronoun 'zû' is an old relative, 'which', which the KJV renders correctly. In an agrarian world where a creditor could seize land, children and body from a poor debtor, the 'scheme' is concrete: false weights, forged debts, a rigged hearing at the gate.

philological_notes.note: 'to burn' and so 'to pursue hotly'. Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all gloss it with Gen 31:36.
An archaic relative particle, 'which', used in poetry (compare Ex 15:13).

verses.translation_literal: For the wicked boasts over the craving of his soul, and one greedy for gain blesses; he spurns YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the wicked man preens over every craving of his own throat, and the profiteer, grasping, gives his blessing — and in the same breath spits on the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the doubt in this verse, because the Hebrew itself is split and the old readers split with it. The verb hillel, 'boasts', is the root of hallelu, 'praise': the wicked man praises himself, and what he praises is the appetite of his own nefesh, his soul, his throat, the part of a person that is always hungry. Then comes a line that can be read two ways. Either the greedy man ('one who cuts off a gain') is the subject of 'blesses' and 'spurns', so that the robber congratulates himself, as Rashi has it, 'I have spurned YHWH and I shall have peace' (the echo of Deut 29:18 is his); this is also the ASV's reading. Or the wicked man blesses the greedy one, praises and honors those who share his road and spurns God, which is the reading of Radak and Meiri and of YLT's 'a dishonest gainer he hath blessed, he hath despised Jehovah'. On both readings the one who spurns YHWH is a wicked or greedy man and never God, and an actor should play it so.

The KJV, 'blesseth the covetous, whom the Lord abhorreth', makes YHWH the one who abhors, but in the Hebrew YHWH is the object, the one spurned: ni'ets is 'treats with contempt' (Metzudat Zion compares 1 Sam 2:17, where men treated the LORD's offering with contempt). The KJV adds a relative clause that the Hebrew lacks and turns an act of contempt toward God into God's verdict on the man.

philological_notes.note: A verb with the accent on the last syllable, 'he blesses'. Rashi argues that it is a verb in the pi'el, 'many such words with the accent on the last syllable behave this way', and not a noun; Ibn Ezra reports another opinion, that berekh is a noun, 'a gift', but calls it incorrect. The ambiguity is in who blesses whom, not in the form.

A participle, 'one who cuts off, who seizes a gain', and so the robber or the profiteer; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'the robber' and compares Hab 2:9. The word 'covetous' in the KJV is milder than 'one who cuts off unjust gain'.
'He spurns, treats with contempt'; the subject is the wicked or greedy man and the object is YHWH. Rashi glosses it as the same as ḥērēf, 'insult'.

verses.translation_literal: A wicked one, according to the height of his nose, [does] not seek; there is no God [in] all his schemes.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked man holds his nose so high that he cannot look for God. 'He will not call me to account.' There is no God: that is the whole of his thinking.
verses.directors_commentary: 'The height of his nose' is the Hebrew idiom, and a good one: the 'nose' (ʾap) stands for the face, and a lifted nose is a lifted chin, the posture of arrogance (Radak and Meiri both cite Gen 42:6, where the brothers bow 'noses' to the ground). The KJV's 'pride of his countenance' translates the idiom into abstraction and keeps nothing of the picture. The verb 'seek' (daraš) has no object in Hebrew, and here the translations part ways: KJV supplies 'after God', ASV and BBE read 'he will not require [it]'. Both are sound, since daraš can mean to seek out God in worship or to hold someone to account (Ps 10:13 uses it for the second sense). The last clause is an ellipsis, 'no God, all his schemes': this is practical atheism, not a philosophical claim; he does not deny that God exists, he plans as if no one will judge. Rashi quotes the rabbinic summary 'there is no judgment and no judge'. Moving the bracket [God] outside the verse would turn the line into a doctrine; keep it a way of living.

philological_notes.note: 'according to the height of his nose'; the face is called the 'nose' because it stands out from it, so a raised nose is arrogance made visible.
'there is no God'. Rashi glosses 'there is no judgment and no judge', which fits the practical sense of the Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: His ways prosper at every time; on high [are] your judgments, from before him; all his foes, he puffs at them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whatever road he takes, it prospers, in every season. Your judgments, LORD, hang so high above him that he never sees them. As for his enemies, he has only to blow, and they are gone.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV and Webster say 'His ways are always grievous', taking yāḥîlû from ḥûl, 'to writhe', which makes the line a complaint about the cruelty of his methods. Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read it from the root of Job 20:21 ('his goods shall not endure'): his ways are firm, they succeed. The context favours the second: the psalm is about the success of the wicked, which is exactly what makes his contempt for God plausible to himself. ASV 'firm' is right, and so is the line's logic: if the wicked never suffer, God's judgments must be far away. 'On high' (mārôm) is the address of God as 'the height'; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as a vocative, 'You are on high', but the sense is the same: your judgments are lofty, out of his line of sight. The last clause is a gesture. 'He puffs at them' is a contemptuous snort, a breath blown at a speck. Actors should show it: the enemies are so little to him that he does not even speak.

philological_notes.note: Two roots compete: ḥûl/ḥîl 'to whirl, writhe' (KJV 'grievous') and a root meaning 'to be firm, to endure, to prosper' (Job 20:21). Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion take the second. STEPBible's 'endure' is close; I gloss 'prosper'.
'to blow, to puff'. Meiri and Rashi take it as a breath that scatters; Radak notes the alternative from 'snare' (paḥ).

verses.translation_literal: He says in his heart, I shall not be shaken; to generation and generation [I shall be] one who [is] not in evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: He says it in his heart, quietly, where only he can hear: 'I will never be shaken. Not in this generation, not in the next: no evil will find me.'
verses.directors_commentary: 'He says in his heart' is the Hebrew way to name a private thought, and it recurs in verses 11 and 13: the psalm eavesdrops on the wicked man's inner monologue. 'Heart' (lēb) is the seat of thinking, not of feeling, so he is not feeling safe; he is reasoning that he is safe. The verb 'shaken' (mwṭ) is the word the psalms use for a foundation giving way (Ps 15:5, 16:8), and the wicked claims for himself the stability the righteous are promised. The last phrase is cryptic, and the KJV smooths it with 'for I shall never be in adversity'. The Hebrew has no 'I' and no 'shall': it reads 'to generation and generation, who not in evil', which the sense of Rashi and Radak resolves as 'I will not come to harm, nor will my descendants'. Malbim adds that he extends the claim to his descendants. The arrogance is generational: he is sure his house will outlast every reversal.

philological_notes.note: 'I shall not be shaken'. The negative bal is poetic and strong, 'never'; the same root describes the immovable righteous in Ps 15:5.
'to generation and generation', an idiom for 'forever', with the descendants in view.

verses.translation_literal: A curse his mouth is full of, and deceits and oppression; under his tongue [are] trouble and wickedness.
verses.translation_dramatic: His mouth is stuffed with oaths and lies and cruelty, and under his tongue lie mischief and harm, waiting.
verses.directors_commentary: The first word 'ʾālâ' is not cursing in the sense of swearing at someone; it is the sworn oath, the formula with a curse attached if the oath is broken. Radak and Metzudat David read it that way: he swears to others with a full mouth to make them believe him, and then deceives them. The KJV 'cursing' loses this: the wicked man's oath is a weapon of fraud. 'Oppression' (tōk) is a rare word, glossed by Rashi as an evil thought lodged within and by Metzudat Zion as hidden deceit; KJV's 'fraud' and ASV's 'oppression' are both guesses at a word that the Hebrew itself leaves close to 'deceit'. The second line gives the picture: 'under the tongue' is the hiding place, as a bitter sweet is held under it (Job 20:12). The mouth is full outside, the venom is stored below. Ancient audiences, who treated oaths as binding and sacred, would hear this as a double sin.

philological_notes.note: A sworn oath with a curse attached; Metzudat Zion cites Lev 5:1. Here it is the wicked man's weapon, not his insult.
A rare noun, 'oppression, fraud'. Rashi takes it as an evil thought hiding within, Metzudat Zion as a deceit hidden in the heart; it forms a pair with mirmâ 'deceit'.

verses.translation_literal: He sits in the ambush of the villages; in the hiding places he kills the innocent; his eyes lie hidden for the unfortunate [one].
verses.translation_dramatic: He sits where the villages lie open, and he waits. In the hiding places, out of every eye, he kills the innocent. His eyes, hooded and patient, keep watch on the helpless.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is of a highwayman, not a tyrant on a throne, and the staging should be small and quiet: a man sitting still beside the road. The hatserim, the 'villages', are not walled towns but unwalled settlements and hamlets scattered along the roads, open to anyone who can sit and watch. Radak supports this and cites Josh 15:45 ('its daughters and its villages'), Isa 42:11 ('the villages that Kedar inhabits') and Zech 2:8 ('Jerusalem shall be inhabited as unwalled villages'); a comparison of my own is Lev 25:31, where houses in villages with no wall around them are treated as open land. Radak adds the bitter point that the wicked man hides from men but not from God who sees everything. Ibn Ezra notes the irony: an ambusher usually sits where no one lives, but this one sits in the settled place.

The verse ends on a rare word, chelekhah. The KJV and ASV smooth it into 'the poor' and 'the helpless', but the Hebrew has an obscure form on which the old interpreters disagree: Rashi reads it as 'your host', as if the innocent were God's own army, while Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as 'the poor, the weak', and the English versions follow them. Notice that the KJV's 'privily set against' is archaic for 'lie hidden': the verb yitzponu means 'to conceal, to store up', and the plural 'eyes' with a plural verb lets the eyes themselves seem to crouch in cover. The KJV's 'lurking places' is fair for ma'arav, 'ambush', but 'villages' alone gives a modern reader no sense that these are open hamlets, which is what gives the verse its menace.

philological_notes.note: Unwalled settlements, 'villages', as against walled towns; Radak calls them 'the open cities that lie along the roads' and cites Josh 15:45, Isa 42:11 and Zech 2:8.

A rare word, uncertain in form and sense. Rashi, relying on the Masorah, takes the -āh as a suffix for -kha, so 'your host'; he also reports Menachem's 'the wretched'. Radak reads ḥelkhāh as ḥēlekh with an added he, 'the poor'. Ibn Ezra relates it to ḥelkha'im ('the wretched'), where Ketiv and Qere disagree about whether it is one word or two.

'They hide, lie concealed'; Radak says it is intransitive: the eyes are placed in a hidden spot and from there watch the roads. Ibn Ezra reports a reading in which the final nun is extra (yitspu, 'they watch').

verses.translation_literal: He lies in wait in the hiding place like a lion in his thicket; he lies in wait to seize the afflicted; he seizes the afflicted by dragging him in his net.
verses.translation_dramatic: He crouches in cover like a lion in his thicket. He waits, and what he waits for is the poor man; and when he has him, he drags him off, caught in his net.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the psalm piles up: 'lies in wait' appears twice, 'the afflicted' twice, 'seize' twice. The repetition is the stalking itself: slow, patient, tightening. The two images are of a lion in its thicket (Radak: the lion stands where prey will pass close, so that it does not flee) and a fowler's net (Radak: the hunter stays far off, a rope in his hand, and pulls it when the bird has entered). The Hebrew word for 'lion' here is ʾaryēh, and the 'thicket' is sōk, the lion's covert; the KJV 'den' makes it a cave, which a lion of the Judean hills would also use, but 'thicket' keeps the ambush. 'Seize' (ḥāṭap) is the swift snatch, Metzudat Zion says, as in Judg 21:21: not a slow hunt but an instant. The poor, the ʿānî, are those the law names again and again as under God's protection; to an audience that knew that, the net is also an insult to God. KJV 'catch' loses the grab.

philological_notes.note: 'to seize swiftly, snatch'. Metzudat Zion compares Judg 21:21; it is the lion's and the bird-catcher's word at once.
A hunting net; Radak describes the fowler holding the ropes from a distance.

verses.translation_literal: He is crushed, he crouches, and [the company of] the wretched fall by his mighty ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: He makes himself small, crushed, crouching low, and then the wretched fall into the grip of his strong ones.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse carries two textual variants and the text is hard, so the actor should know where the ground is soft. The Qere reads yidkeh, 'he is crushed'; the Ketiv wĕdakkâ is a variant of the same sense. Rashi, Radak and Meiri read it as the predator's disguise: he makes himself look crushed and bent, like a sick traveller, so that his victims drop their guard; the lion of v. 9 crouches too (Ibn Ezra). The second half has another Ketiv/Qere: written as one word ḥēlkāʾîm, read as two, ḥēl kāʾîm, 'a company of the crushed' (Rashi, citing the Masorah). The ʿăṣûmāyw is 'his mighty ones': the gang. Radak says that the wicked man and his band feign illness and weakness, then show their strength when far from help. The KJV 'he croucheth and humbleth himself' reads it right, but 'that the poor may fall' turns a description into a purpose clause the Hebrew lacks; and the Hebrew's 'fall' (nāpal) is the one used for dying on the battlefield. It is the scene of a mugging, with an actor's alibi: the bent figure who looks harmless.

philological_notes.note: Written as one word, read as two (ḥēl kāʾîm, 'company of the crushed'). Rashi gives the Masoretic list of such words; Menahem takes it as one word meaning 'poor and weak', from the same root as ḥēlkâ in v. 8.

'by his mighty ones' (Rashi's second reading, his strong men). Rashi's first reading, from 'to shut the eyes', takes it as his winks and signals; Ibn Ezra reads 'his bones', meaning his powerful limbs.

verses.translation_literal: He says in his heart, God has forgotten; he has hidden his face; he has not seen, for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: And again, deep in his heart, he says: 'God has forgotten. He has covered his face. He will never see it, not ever.'
verses.directors_commentary: The wicked man's third private speech (vv. 4, 6, 11, and again in 13) answers the speaker's own complaint in v. 1: the psalmist accused God of hiding, and the wicked man turns the accusation into an argument. 'Forgotten' and 'hidden face' are the verbs of lament: the same vocabulary, in the wrong mouth. Notice the escalation, which Malbim lays out: God has forgotten, then hidden his face, then cannot see at all. The KJV 'he will never see it' adds 'it' (the Hebrew has no object) and 'will' (the Hebrew is a perfect: 'he has not seen for ever'), turning a settled conclusion into a prediction. The word translated 'for ever' is lāneṣaḥ, which can also mean 'to the end, completely'. Ibn Ezra's point is important: this man does not deny that God exists; he denies that God knows. Directors: this is the bitter irony of the scene; the wicked and the psalmist are using the same words, and only one of them is right.

philological_notes.note: 'he has hidden his face'. A stock phrase for divine absence in lament (Ps 13:2; 27:9); the speaker of v. 1 says God 'hides' and the wicked repeats it as a fact.
'for ever, to perpetuity'; can also mean 'completely'. The perfect tense of bal rāʾâ gives a settled conclusion, not a prediction.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, YHWH! God, lift up your hand! Do not forget the humble.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, LORD! O God, lift up your hand! Do not forget the humble.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn. After eleven verses of description the psalm erupts into three short imperatives, and the first, qûmâ, 'arise', is the old war-cry of the ark (Num 10:35): God is called to get up from where he has been sitting or standing at a distance (v. 1). 'Lift up your hand' is the gesture of an oath or of a blow: Ibn Ezra says it shows power, and Radak and Metzudat David read it as raising the hand against the wicked. The KJV 'forget not the humble' is accurate and keeps the answer to the wicked man's 'God has forgotten' in v. 11: the verb is the same, šākaḥ, one clause denying it of God, the next praying that it not be so. The word 'humble' reflects a Qere, ʿănāwîm; the Ketiv is ʿănîyîm, 'poor', and Radak says it was the older writing. The two words overlap: the afflicted poor are those who are humble before God, which is why the psalm uses both. The KJV and ASV differ here ('humble' against 'poor'), and neither is wrong.

philological_notes.note: 'lift up your hand', the gesture of power or an oath. Ibn Ezra: raising the hand shows strength; Radak and Metzudat David: raised against the wicked.
'do not forget', answering the wicked man's 'God has forgotten' (šākaḥ ʾēl) in v. 11 with the same verb.

verses.translation_literal: On what has [the] wicked spurned God? He has said in his heart: You will not seek.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why? Why does the wicked man spit on God and walk away unpunished? Because he has told himself, deep in his chest where no one hears: You will never come looking.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the psalm's hinge. The poet turns from describing the predator to asking the question underneath: what makes a man bold enough to treat God with contempt? The answer is a private sentence, said 'in his heart', the seat of thought and will in Hebrew. Nobody hears it; the whole psalm has been the story of that unspoken line (the same words as v.4, 'there is no God', now sharpened into 'you will not seek').

The verb נאץ means to scorn or treat as worthless, not merely to 'contemn'. The KJV's 'contemn' is a Latinate word that has almost vanished, and 'Thou wilt not require it' hides that the Hebrew has no 'it' and uses דרשׁ, the same verb that means to inquire, investigate and hold accountable. The wicked man's creed is that God keeps no ledger. Play it as a defendant's whisper, not a shout: his contempt is calm because he thinks no one is watching.

philological_notes.note: To scorn, treat with contempt; the offense is dismissing someone's authority, not cursing in anger. Elsewhere used of spurning a covenant or God's counsel.

To seek, inquire, and so to require an account. The wicked man's claim is that God will not investigate. The same root returns in v.15 ('you will seek his wickedness'), where God answers the claim by doing exactly what the wicked said he would not.

verses.translation_literal: You have seen, for you — trouble and vexation you look at, to give [it] in your hand. On you the wretched one leaves [himself]; the fatherless, you have been a helper.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have seen it. You see everything. The trouble they cause, the grief that burns in the people they crush: you look straight at it, and it is in your hand to repay. So the wretched leave their cause with you, because the fatherless have always found you at their side.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist now answers the wicked man's whisper, and the voice changes from complaint to confidence. 'You have seen' is a flat contradiction of 'you will not seek'. The speaker is not guessing; he is stating what he knows of God's character.

The KJV smooths the verse into 'to requite it with thy hand', which is a fair guess at לָתֵת בְּיָדֶךָ, literally 'to put/give into your hand', and 'the poor committeth himself unto thee', which is a defensible reading of עָלֶיךָ יַעֲזֹב חֵלֶכָה. But the Hebrew is blunter: 'on you he leaves' leaves the object unspoken, so the listener supplies it, whether his burden, his lawsuit or himself. Metzudat David and Radak take it as the poor man handing his case to God. In the ancient world the fatherless had no legal protector, no father to speak for them at the gate, which is why 'helper of the fatherless' is a title God claims in the Torah's law. Say it as one who has watched this happen before.

philological_notes.note: Two words for the damage a wrongdoer causes: 'amal is toil and the trouble inflicted on others; ka'as is vexation or provocation. STEPBible's 'mischief' is too light; the pair means the suffering of the victims together with the anger of the aggressor.
A rare word for a helpless or unfortunate person, found in this psalm (vv.8, 10, 14) and nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Radak explains the final ה as added to an existing form.

A helper. The verb in the previous clause, יַעֲזֹב, 'leaves/abandons', comes from a different root (עזב) but sounds almost the same, so the line plays 'the wretched leaves it to you; you are the one who helps'. Rashi connects עזב here with the 'help' sense.

verses.translation_literal: Break [the] arm of [the] wicked, and [the] evil — you will seek his wickedness; you will not find.
verses.translation_dramatic: Break the arm of the wicked. Break the strength that crushes. And then go looking, LORD, as he said you never would. Search out his wickedness, and find nothing left.
verses.directors_commentary:
The arm is the ancient image of power: the arm that lifts the sword, the oppressor's means of seizing land and grain. To break it is to end the capacity to harm, and the psalmist asks for it as a plain command, an imperative addressed straight to God.

The second half hands the wicked man's own word back to him. He said 'you will not seek' (v.13); now the same verb tidrosh is spoken to God as a promise: you will seek, and what you seek 'you will not find'. The KJV's 'till thou find none' adds a conjunction and a quantity that are not there; the Hebrew simply stops, and the silence is the point. Commentators differ on what disappears: the wickedness itself (Radak, Metzudat David) or the arm. Let the actor leave the final phrase hanging.

philological_notes.note: Arm, as the seat of strength and violence. 'Breaking the arm' is a standard image for destroying an enemy's power.
'Seek' and 'not find' form a pair. The reversal of v.13's 'you will not seek' is deliberate; the poem answers the wicked man in his own vocabulary.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] king forever and ever; nations have perished from his land.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is king, now and for ever. The nations have vanished from his land.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the prayer, a shout of confidence, and the mood shifts suddenly from pleading to declaration. 'YHWH is king' is the oldest political claim in the psalter: the god of Israel, not any human monarch or foreign god, holds the throne, and it holds 'forever and ever' (עוֹלָם וָעֶד), which means time out of sight in both directions.

The second clause is in the perfect tense: 'have perished'. The KJV renders גּוֹיִם as 'the heathen', a word with a later Christian ring; the Hebrew is simply 'nations', the foreign peoples who occupy or threaten the land. Whether the psalmist speaks of past victories (the Canaanite peoples of the conquest, as Metzudat David reads it) or of a future he is already certain of (a 'prophetic perfect', as Radak and Meiri read it) is unresolved; say the line with the certainty that makes the question unnecessary. 'His land' is God's land, not Israel's, a claim of ownership every audience understood.

philological_notes.note: They have perished, been lost. The perfect can mean a completed event or a certainty spoken as already done; the commentators take it both ways.
Nations, peoples; not specifically 'pagans' or 'heathen' as the KJV translates it. Here the foreign nations who do not recognise YHWH.

verses.translation_literal: The desire of [the] humble ones you have heard, YHWH; you establish their heart, you cause your ear to attend,
verses.translation_dramatic: You have heard it, LORD, the longing of the humble, the wish too low to be spoken aloud. You steady their heart as it trembles. You bend your ear and listen.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns from the cry of the previous verses to confidence, and the actor should let the voice settle. The 'humble' (anavim) are not merely meek: they are people pressed down by the powerful, so their only resource is a God who listens. The word 'desire' (ta'avah) is usually a craving, so the line has a daring edge: even their unspoken longing reaches him. Radak even reads it as God hearing the wish before their mouths utter it, citing Isaiah 65:24.

The KJV turns the verbs into future promises, 'thou wilt prepare their heart, thou wilt cause thine ear to hear'. The Hebrew has a perfect ('you have heard') and then two imperfects ('you establish', 'you cause to attend'), which read as God's settled way of acting. 'Establish' (from kun) is the word for setting something firm, as one sets a foundation. The last phrase is a causative: God makes his own ear attentive. Ibn Ezra notes that the verb can be read either as 'you cause your ear to attend' or as 'your ear attends', with the taw as a feminine marker, since 'ear' is feminine. Either way the ear is the point, and the line says it twice, once in the verb and once in the noun.

philological_notes.note: Desire, craving, longing. It is often negative elsewhere, which makes it striking that God hears the longing of the humble. Radak reads it as the prayer matching their desire, or the desire heard before it is voiced.
Hiphil of kun, 'to set firm, establish'. Radak understands it as God removing the world's distractions from their heart so they can pray with intent.
Hiphil of qashav, 'to cause to attend', with 'your ear' as object. Ibn Ezra reads the taw as a feminine marker with 'ear' as subject, so the sense is the same either way: God's ear is attentive.

verses.translation_literal: To judge [the] fatherless and [the] crushed, [so that] he will not add again to terrify, man, from the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Justice for the orphan, justice for the crushed. Let mortal man, dust of the earth, never again make anyone tremble.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse says what the humble ask God to hear. 'To judge' (shaphat) here means to give a verdict that rescues, to take up a case and put it right, as Radak and Metzudat David say: to take their judgment from the hands of those who robbed them. The fatherless and the 'crushed' (dakh) are the classic people without protection in the ancient Near East: with no father or patron to speak for them at the city gate, they had no one to claim their rights. Rashi reads it as Israel's own case, and the last phrase 'man from the earth' as aimed at Esau.

The closing words carry a sting that translations soften. 'Enosh' is frail, mortal man, the word that stresses weakness, set against the God who is king. So the psalm ends by shrinking the terror: a man 'from the earth' is only dust, and cannot go on frightening people. The KJV 'that the man of the earth may no more oppress' turns 'terrify' into the milder 'oppress' and makes 'of the earth' a description of him, not a place. The verb arats means to strike with dread, and the Hebrew idiom is 'he will not add again to terrify'. Metzudat Zion links it to breaking; Ibn Ezra and Meiri allow also 'to fear man', with 'from the earth' either way pointing to man's earthly nature. Play the last line low and quiet: the tyrant is being made small.

philological_notes.note: To strike with dread, terrify. Radak takes it as transitive, citing Isaiah 2:19. Ibn Ezra and Meiri also allow 'to fear' (as in Deuteronomy 1:29), which would turn the line into 'no more to be afraid of man'.
Crushed, oppressed, one who has been ground down. Metzudat Zion glosses it as thin and tormented.

'Man from the earth': the word enosh stresses frailty and mortality, and 'from the earth' sets his origin as dust, against the heavenly king of verse 16. Whether it means a man 'of the earth' or 'from the land', the sense is that his power is merely human.
